claims.text: Wear resistance in HEA protective coatings is primarily governed by sliding-induced formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline or amorphous/nanocrystalline surface layer.
The transformed surface layer improves wear resistance by combining high shear strength with homogeneous deformability.
The initial coating has a relatively coarse-grained or mixed-phase microstructure.
Changing load and oxygen availability can promote or suppress dynamic transformation of the sliding surface.
Dynamic amorphization occurs only when applied stress exceeds a threshold.
There is a temperature range in which the proposed shear-driven transformations are feasible.
Sliding transforms the near-surface region into an ultra-nanocrystalline or amorphous/nanocrystalline layer with refined grain boundaries.
Mechanical shear during sliding triggers dynamic refinement or amorphization of the surface microstructure.
Reactive oxidation during sliding can form an amorphous-crystalline oxide nanocomposite surface layer.
The transformed layer increases resistance to further deformation and crack propagation.
Formation of the ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer lowers friction and wear.
Coatings that form the transformed layer will have significantly lower friction and wear than otherwise comparable coatings in which transformation is absent or suppressed.
Lower loads prevent dynamic transformation and preserve the original coarse-grained microstructure.
Inert conditions prevent shear- or oxide-driven surface transformation.
Failure to form the transformed layer results in higher wear rates and friction.
The mechanism operates only over shear-stress and oxygen-partial-pressure ranges sufficient to trigger surface transformation.
Very high or very low oxygen availability, very low applied stress, or insufficient plastic deformation can place the system outside the mechanism's effective range.
The relative contributions of mechanical shear and reactive oxidation to layer formation are not established.
Statistically indistinguishable wear and friction between samples with verified inhibition of layer formation and untreated samples would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The conditions field allows transformation under inert environments when load is sufficient, whereas the baseline states that inert conditions prevent shear- or oxide-driven transformation. Inertness can suppress oxidation but does not inherently suppress mechanical shear transformation.
